levels.101.lesson.phases.intro.text: Rows and columns, 1 to 4, each exactly once. That is the only rule.
levels.101.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Shen Mo’s eyes land on the empty cell at the top right of the card—c2. This row already has 1, 4, and 2.
levels.101.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: This cell is 1. c2 cannot be 1.
levels.101.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: This cell is 4. c2 cannot be 4 either.
levels.101.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: This cell is 2. c2 cannot be 2 either.
levels.101.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: Looking at one row is not enough. He scans the column c2 sits in—numbers there block the way too.
levels.101.lesson.phases.demo.steps.6.te: The column has a 2, ruling out another possibility.
levels.101.lesson.phases.demo.steps.7.te: The column has a 4, ruling out one more.
levels.101.lesson.phases.demo.steps.8.te: There it is—1, 4, and 2 are all ruled out, leaving 3. Only one number satisfies both the row and the column. c2 can only be 3.
levels.101.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Shen Mo’s pen hovers over the first empty cell. The numbers already in its row and column… remove them, and what remains is the answer.
levels.101.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 2-cell cage sums to 7 and the other cells add up to 4—subtract what's filled: what should c2 be?
levels.101.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Shen Mo looks again… this row already has it, this column already has it. He rules out everything impossible, and what is left is correct.
levels.101.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Shen Mo sets down his pen. The first cell is filled. Decoding this letter begins here.
levels.101.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Good, once more: d4’s row has a 4, its column has 3 and 2… after ruling those out, what is left? Try it.
Now a4: this column already has 3, 2, and the 1 you just filled. Rule them out and only one number remains—try it.
levels.101.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the same method to find two more numbers.
levels.101.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: Walk the rest of the way yourself.
levels.102.lesson.phases.intro.text: A 4×4 grid. In every row, every column, and every thick-bordered box, 1 to 4 appear exactly once.
levels.102.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: Vera gives no more hints. He must piece together the 4×4 constraints himself—each thick-outlined 2×2 block is a “box,” and 1 to 4 appear exactly once inside it.
levels.102.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: He looks at a3: it is inside a box. The box already has 4 and 2, so a3 can only be 1 or 3.
levels.102.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: The 4 of this box is here.
levels.102.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: This cell is 2, so a3 cannot be 2.
levels.102.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: Now the column a3 sits in: it already has 2 and 3 below—a3 cannot be 3 either.
levels.102.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: The box only leaves 1 and 3, and the column rules out 3—a3 must be 1. Box rule: check the box and the column, eliminating numbers already present.
levels.102.lesson.phases.guided.autoReve: a3 is in a box: the box has 4 and 2, needing 1 and 3; this column already has 3—so a3 can only be 1.
levels.102.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 4-cell cage sums to 10 with 4 already filled, so a3 must pair with the remaining empty cells to make 6. Eliminate what the row/column/box rules out—what's left is your answer. Try it.
levels.102.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Shen Mo pauses… this row already has that number. He cannot place the same number twice in a row.
levels.102.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Shen Mo sets down his pen. The 4×4 lock is open.
levels.102.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: With the same method, look at these empty cells.
levels.102.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: Use all three rules together. Walk the rest of the way yourself.
levels.103.lesson.phases.intro.text: A 4×4 grid with cage sums. The numbers inside each dashed cage add up to the number in its corner. This is a verification puzzle—confirming what you hold is real.
levels.103.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: Shen Mo’s gaze lands on the dashed cage—it encloses 4 cells, and the 10 in its corner is their total sum.
levels.103.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Inside are b2, c2, c3, and d3. He checks each one by one.
levels.103.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: He checks c3’s row: row 2 already has 2 and 1, so c3 can only be 3 or 4.
levels.103.lesson.phases.demo.steps.6.te: Now the column: it already has 3, ruling 3 out of c3—only 4 remains! He checks every cell, careful not to miss any.
levels.103.lesson.phases.guided.autoReve: c3 is in a dashed cage: this row already has 2 and 1, needing 3 and 4; this column already has 3—so c3 can only be 4.
levels.103.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 4-cell cage sums to 10 with 4 already filled, so c3 must pair with the remaining empty cells to make 6. Eliminate what the row/column/box rules out—what's left is your answer. Try it.
levels.103.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Shen Mo recalculates… if this number is wrong, the whole puzzle’s validity falls apart.
levels.103.lesson.phases.guided.successT: The 7 is set. Verification passed. This copy of War and Peace truly is the teacher’s signpost.
levels.103.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Look at two more cells: b3 only has 1 left; c4 and d4 share a cage summing to 4—column 3 has 2, row 2 has 1, leaving only 3. Try it.
levels.103.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: The cage sum is a sharp tool. Walk the rest of the way yourself.
levels.104.lesson.phases.intro.text: When unsure, write down all candidates. Notes are the wall you can feel in the dark.
levels.104.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: Shen Mo marks every possible number beside c4 and d4—they share a cage summing to 3, so only 1 and 2 are possible.
levels.104.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: Now row 3: it already has 2 and 4, ruling 2 out of c4—leaving only 1. The column has it, the row has it, only one remains, and it is right here.
levels.104.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: He taps the Notes button first and jots candidate 1 in c4; when he fills the number, that note will be crossed out automatically.
levels.104.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Shen Mo’s pen pauses over the middle empty cell. He writes down every possibility beside it… then rules them out one by one.
levels.104.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Jot notes in c4: the 2-cell cage sums to 3; after eliminating row/column/box, which candidates remain? Write them down.
levels.104.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Shen Mo stops writing… this cell cannot take that number. He missed a candidate that is already present.
levels.104.lesson.phases.guided.successT: All notes exhausted. Only one number fits this empty cell. Shen Mo confirms it.
levels.104.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Once more: a2’s row needs 1, 2, 4, and its column has 2; it shares a cage with b2 (sum 10, 2 and 4 already filled, leaving two cells totaling 4—only 1 and 3)—ruled down to 1. d3 and d2 share a cage summing to 7 (3 and 4), row has 1, column has 4—leaving 3.
levels.104.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: Notes are a good helper. Walk the rest slowly.
levels.105.lesson.phases.intro.text: In a 4×4 grid, two-cell cage sums have only four unique combinations: 3=1+2, 4=1+3, 6=2+4, 7=3+4.
levels.105.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: Shen Mo reads the two-cell cage at a glance: its corner is 7, so the pair must be 3 and 4—the “seven takes three-four” rule.
levels.105.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Now column 4, where these cells sit: 2 and 4 are already above, so 4 cannot go here—the lower cell is ruled out.
levels.105.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: The rule gives 3 and 4, and the column rules out 4—this cell must be 3! A unique cage sum means a unique number. Shen Mo writes it down.
levels.105.lesson.phases.guided.autoReve: This two-cell cage sums to 7—“seven takes three-four” gives 3 and 4; this column already has 4, so enter 3.
levels.105.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 2-cell cage sums to 7 with 0 already filled, so d4 must pair with the remaining empty cells to make 7. Eliminate what the row/column/box rules out—what's left is your answer. Try it.
levels.105.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Shen Mo pauses… are there other combinations for this sum? He counts again—no.
levels.105.lesson.phases.guided.successT: 3 and 4 are set. Shen Mo puts down his pen. He has passed Vera’s first test of trust.
levels.105.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Again: c4’s cage sums to 3 (“three takes one-two”), this column has 2, so c4 is 1; d3 and d4 share a cage summing to 7, 7−3=4, so d3 is 4.
levels.105.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: The rule is memorized. You will use it often on the road ahead.
levels.106.lesson.phases.intro.text: Do not just count candidates per cell. Scan the numbers—find the one with only a single path left on the whole board.
levels.106.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: Shen Mo scans the number 4 across the board—the top-left box still needs 1, 2, 3, 4, and 4 can only go in one spot.
levels.106.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: First, row 1: it has 1 and 3, needing 2 and 4.
levels.106.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: Now column 2: c2 already holds 4, so 4 cannot go in this column—the cell in row 1, column 2 is ruled out.
levels.106.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: After elimination, 4 has only a1 left in row 1—this is the Hidden Radiance. Shen Mo fills it.
levels.106.lesson.phases.guided.autoReve: a1 is in row 1: the row needs 2 and 4, but column 2 already has 4—so a1 can only be 4.
levels.106.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Shen Mo’s gaze rests on 4. It has only two spots in its row, and one is blocked in the column… leaving a single cell. That is it.
levels.106.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Shen Mo scans again… he missed a cell. The 4 there was already ruled out.
levels.106.lesson.phases.guided.successT: The 4 is set. The Hidden Radiance is found. It is the hinge of this puzzle—once fixed, the other numbers loosen up.
levels.106.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the number-scanning method to find two more Hidden Radiance cells.
levels.106.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: Hidden Radiance hides deep, but it can always be found.
levels.107.lesson.phases.intro.text: The lock on the iron door is a puzzle. Solve it wrong and the door will not open; when time runs out, the footsteps will arrive first.
levels.107.lesson.phases.guided.autoReve: The three-cell cage a4, b4, b3 sums to 6, and b4 is already 3—leaving 6−3=3, so the pair can only be 1 and 2; row a already has a2=1, so a4 must be 2.
levels.107.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 3-cell cage sums to 6 with 3 already filled, so a4 must pair with the remaining empty cells to make 3. Eliminate what the row/column/box rules out—what's left is your answer. Try it.
levels.107.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Shen Mo pauses… this cell cannot take that number. He checks the cage sum again.
levels.107.lesson.phases.guided.successT: The single-cell cage is set. Shen Mo does not stop—he keeps filling, hearing the echo of footsteps at the alley mouth.
levels.107.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the same method to find two more numbers.
levels.107.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: Unique combinations are now second nature. Walk the rest of the way yourself.
levels.108.lesson.phases.intro.text: In a 4×4 grid, every row, column, and box sums to exactly 10. This is the deepest constraint—and your final verification.
levels.108.lesson.phases.guided.autoReve: The three-cell cage a1, b1, c1 sums to 6, and b1 is already 3—the remaining pair sums to 3, only 1 and 2; row a already has a2=4 and a3=2, so a1 must be 1.
levels.108.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 3-cell cage sums to 6 with 3 already filled, so a1 must pair with the remaining empty cells to make 3. Eliminate what the row/column/box rules out—what's left is your answer. Try it.
levels.108.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Shen Mo does the math… the row’s numbers already exceed 10. He must have made an error somewhere earlier.
levels.108.lesson.phases.guided.successT: The whole row adds up to 10. Shen Mo sets down his pen. He has passed all three tests of trust.
levels.108.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the Rule of 10 and cage sums to find two more certain numbers.
levels.108.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: The Rule of 10 is the master key and a sharp tool for verification. Walk the rest of the way yourself.
levels.109.lesson.phases.intro.text: A 6×6 board. This is no ordinary level—it is the Touchstone. Every number you fill right claims a hub; three in a line seals the win.
levels.109.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: First, the board rules: the highlighted cells are “hubs”—fill them right and you score in all four dimensions (row, column, box, cage); control three dimensions and the hub is yours.
levels.109.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: The first key is here—the single-cell cage “Lone Star”: only one cell, sum 4, so it must be 4. Fill it and the hubs start tipping your way.
levels.109.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: Remember how to win: ① claim hubs—take all three; ② three in a line—line up the three hubs for an instant kill; ③ or fill the board and outcount. The AI is grabbing too—do not let it connect.
levels.109.lesson.phases.guided.autoReve: This single-cell cage sums to 4, so enter 4.
levels.109.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: The “Lone Star” single-cell cage: one cell, and whatever the sum is, that is the number. Fill it first—this is the starting point.
levels.109.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: f4 is a single-cell cage—its sum 4 IS the number to fill. What is it?
levels.109.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Shen Mo recalculates… this cell cannot take that number. He looks back at the row and finds he missed one.
levels.109.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Shen Mo sets down his pen. The 6×6 board is fully closed. Every clue has run its course in his hands—from the first 4×4 to this final 6×6, each step connects.
levels.109.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Keep claiming hub cells: this two-cell cage sums to 5, and the right cell is already 3—what goes left? Fill it right and your hub count goes +1!
Again! This two-cell cage sums to 5, and the lower cell is 1—fill this one and pull the hub to your side!
levels.109.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Keep pushing: every number you confirm earns dimension points toward your hubs. Find three more certain numbers.
levels.109.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: Lesson over. Now it is a duel: claim hubs, block the line, or fill the board. The matter of June ends with this game.
levels.201.lesson.phases.intro.text: Welcome to the 6×6 board! Numbers are 1-6. Watch this row—its digits always add up to 21. Subtract the known numbers from 21, and what remains is the answer!
levels.201.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: Look at row a: 4, 1, 2, 3, 6 already fill five cells. In a 6×6 board every row must hold 1-6, always summing to 21.
levels.201.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Row a only lacks a6. 21 − 4 − 1 − 2 − 3 − 6 = 5, so a6 is 5! This is the Row Star-Balance Law.
levels.201.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Row Star-Balance: every row in a 6×6 board sums to 21. Row a has 4, 1, 2, 3, 6, lacking only a6—subtract from 21 to get 5.
levels.201.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: row a already has 4, 1, 2, 3, 6 and only a6 is empty. Every row in a 6×6 board sums to 21—subtract what's filled: what should a6 be?
levels.201.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Look at row 1: 4+1+2+3+6=16, 21−16=5, so the empty cell is 5!
levels.201.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! The Star-Balance Law locks in the answer.
levels.201.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the Star-Balance Law to find two more cells.
levels.202.lesson.phases.intro.text: Columns work the same way! Every column also sums to 21. Look at this column and subtract the known numbers from 21.
levels.202.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: Now the column! Column f already has 1, 4, 2, 6, 3. Like a row, its total is always 21.
levels.202.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Column f only lacks a6. 21 − 1 − 4 − 2 − 6 − 3 = 5, so a6 is 5! This is the Column Star-Balance Law—identical to the row rule, just rotated.
levels.202.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Column Star-Balance: every column sums to 21. Column f has 1, 4, 2, 6, 3, lacking only a6—subtract from 21 to get 5. Identical to the row rule, just rotated.
levels.202.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: row a already has 4, 1, 2, 3, 6 and only a6 is empty. Every row in a 6×6 board sums to 21—subtract what's filled: what should a6 be?
levels.202.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Look at column f: 1+4+2+6+3=16, 21−16=5, so the empty cell is 5!
levels.202.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! The Column Star-Balance Law locks in the answer.
levels.202.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the Star-Balance Law to find two more cells.
levels.203.lesson.phases.intro.text: Boxes are no exception! Every 2×3 box also sums to 21. Box, row, and column all follow the Star-Balance Law.
levels.203.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: Look at the top-right box: 6, 5, 4, 2 already fill four cells. Every 2×3 box sums to 21—so a4 and b6 together total 4, meaning only 1 and 3.
levels.203.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Now row a: 1, 2, 6, 5 are already present, so a4 can only be 3 or 4. Combined with the box’s 1 or 3—the intersection is 3! a4 is 3. This is the Box Star-Balance Law.
levels.203.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Box Star-Balance: every 2×3 box sums to 21. The top-right box has 6, 5, 4, 2, leaving a4 and b6 totaling 4 (only 1 and 3); row a has 1, 2, 6, 5, so a4 can only be 3 or 4—the intersection is 3!
levels.203.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 2-cell cage sums to 5 and the other cells add up to 2—subtract what's filled: what should a4 be?
levels.203.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Look at the top-right box: 6+5+4+2=17, 21−17=4, so a4 and b6 total 4. Row a has 1, 2, 6, 5, so a4 is 3 or 4—the intersection is 3!
levels.203.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! The Box Star-Balance Law locks in the answer.
levels.203.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the Star-Balance Law to find two more cells.
levels.204.lesson.phases.intro.text: The board is now 9×9! Every row, column, and box sums to 45. Subtract the known numbers from 45, and what remains is the answer.
levels.204.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Look at this row (or column, box): 45 minus the sum of known numbers gives the empty cell.
levels.204.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! Keep going with the Star-Balance Law.
levels.204.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the Star-Balance Law to find two more cells.
levels.205.lesson.phases.intro.text: The Star-Balance Law can pin down a single cell: combine all four constraints—row, column, box, cage—and the unique intersection is the answer.
levels.205.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: Look at row d: it has 3, 9, 1, 7, 8. This row lacks 2, 4, 5, 6.
levels.205.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: d3 also sits in a cage summing to 9 (c3+d3+d4), and c3 is 2, so d3 and d4 total 7. Column 3 lacks 3, 4, 6, 7, and the box lacks 4, 6, 9—the intersection of row, column, box, and cage leaves only 6! d3 is 6.
levels.205.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Multi-constraint intersection: d3 is in a cage summing to 9 (c3 is 2, so d3+d4=7); row d lacks 2, 4, 5, 6; column 3 lacks 3, 4, 6, 7; the box lacks 4, 6, 9—all four intersect at only 6!
levels.205.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 3-cell cage sums to 9 and the other cells add up to 3—subtract what's filled: what should d3 be?
levels.205.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: d3’s cage sums to 9 (c3 is 2, leaving d3+d4=7). Row d lacks 2, 4, 5, 6, column 3 lacks 3, 4, 6, 7, the box lacks 4, 6, 9—the intersection is 6!
levels.205.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! Four constraints intersect to lock the answer.
levels.205.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the Star-Balance Law to find two more cells.
levels.206.lesson.phases.intro.text: When two cages nest, use the difference: the gap between the two sums equals the value of the overlapping cell.
levels.206.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Compare the two cage sums—the difference points to the certain number in the overlapping cell.
levels.206.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! Keep going with the Star-Balance Law.
levels.206.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the Star-Balance Law to find two more cells.
levels.207.lesson.phases.intro.text: When a cage crosses a box boundary, the cell outside the box can be found with Box Star-Balance—subtract the in-box cage sums from 45.
levels.207.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Start with the box total 45, subtract the in-box cage sums, and what remains is the cell outside the box.
levels.207.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! Keep going with the Star-Balance Law.
levels.207.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the Star-Balance Law to find two more cells.
levels.208.lesson.phases.intro.text: The final trial—Ito himself joins you on the board! You can see his numbers (with a glow), and you can steal back the cells he fills wrong. Use row, column, box, cage, and difference—win this duel! [Cipher extraction] Besides filling the board, you must also correctly complete all hidden target cells to extract the cipher.
levels.208.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: Look at row i: it has 5, 7, 4. This row lacks 1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 9.
levels.208.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: i1 is in column 1 (has 6, 8, 7, 9, lacking 1, 2, 3, 4, 5). Combine the cage sum and box elimination—the intersection leaves only 1! Fill i1 with 1, before Ito does!
levels.208.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Synthesis Star-Balance: row i lacks 1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 9; column 1 lacks 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; add the cage sum and box elimination—only 1 remains!
levels.208.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 3-cell cage sums to 13 and the other cells add up to 12—subtract what's filled: what should i1 be?
levels.208.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Row i lacks 1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 9, column 1 lacks 1, 2, 3, 4, 5—intersection is 1, 2, 3; with i1’s cage sum and box constraints, only 1 works!
levels.208.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! This cell is yours—keep claiming, do not let Ito get ahead!
levels.208.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the Star-Balance Law to find two more cells.
levels.301.lesson.phases.intro.text: Row block: when a number in a box can only sit in one row, that number is ruled out from the rest of the row. This is Pointing Elimination.
levels.301.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: Look at the middle-right box. Let us track where 4 can go inside it.
levels.301.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: e4 is already 4, so no empty cell in row e inside this box can be 4.
levels.301.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: h9 is also 4, so column 9 in this box is likewise ruled out for 4.
levels.301.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: Count it: where can 4 go in this box now? Only d7 and d8.
levels.301.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: Mark 4 on d7 and d8—both in row d! This is a Row Block.
levels.301.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: Since 4 can only sit in row d inside the box, no cell of row d outside the box can be 4—including d3!
levels.301.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Row Block in three steps: find a number in a box, see if it can only land in one row; if so, eliminate it from the rest of that row.
levels.301.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: d3’s candidates are only 4 and 8, and the Row Block pins 4 to d7 and d8—try it. What goes in d3?
levels.301.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Wait—the 4 in this box can only go in row d, so no cell of row d outside the box can hold 4. With 4 eliminated, d3 is 8.
levels.301.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! That is Row Block elimination—the box constrains the row, the row deletes the rest.
levels.301.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Great! Now e8: the row has 7, 6, 4, 2, 9, 8, the column has 9, 3, 5, the box still has 9, 8, 2, 5—only 1 remains. Enter 1!
Again! g1: the row has 1, 3, 5, the column has 8, 6, 4, 9, 7, the box still has 1, 8—only 2 remains. Enter 2!
levels.301.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the Row Block method to find two more numbers.
levels.302.lesson.phases.intro.text: Column block: when a number in a box can only sit in one column, it is ruled out from the rest of that column—the mirror of a Row Block.
levels.302.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: Look at the bottom-middle box. Let us track where the number 9 can go inside it.
levels.302.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: i3 is already 9, so no empty cell in row i inside this box can be 9.
levels.302.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: e6 is also 9, so in column 6, g6 and h6 inside this box are also ruled out for 9.
levels.302.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: The note 9 appears on g6 and h6 first; then look at this column—they are eliminated.
levels.302.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: Cross out the 9 on g6 and h6: these two cells cannot be 9.
levels.302.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: Count it: where can 9 go in this box now? Only g5 and h5—both in column 5! This is a Column Block.
levels.302.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Column Block in three steps: find a number in a box, see if it can only land in one column; if so, eliminate it from the rest of that column.
levels.302.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: a5’s candidates are only 3 and 9, and the Column Block pins 9 to g5 and h5—try it. What goes in a5?
levels.302.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Wait—the 9 in this box can only go in column 5, so no cell of column 5 outside the box can hold 9. With 9 eliminated, a5 is 3.
levels.302.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! That is Column Block elimination—the box constrains the column, the column deletes the rest.
levels.302.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Great! Now b3: the row has 1, 4, 7, the column has 2, 6, 5, 7, 9, the box still has 7, 8, 2, 1—only 3 remains. Enter 3!
Again! With b3 filled, look at c3: the box now has 7, 8, 2, 1, 3, the column has 2, 6, 5, 7, 9—only 4 remains. Enter 4!
levels.302.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the Column Block method to find two more numbers.
levels.303.lesson.phases.intro.text: Box block (row/column to box): when a number in a row or column can only land in one box, it is ruled out from the rest of that box.
levels.303.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: Look at column 6 first. Where can 2 go in this column?
levels.303.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Both a6 and b6 have 2 among their candidates.
levels.303.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: In column 6, 2 can only sit in a6 and b6, both in the top box—this is a Box Block.
levels.303.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: Look at a4: only 2 and 6 remain (mark 2 for now).
levels.303.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Box Block in three steps: find a number in a row or column, see if it can only land in one box; if so, eliminate it from the rest of that box.
levels.303.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: a4’s candidates are only 2 and 6, and the Box Block pins 2 to a6 and b6—try it. What goes in a4?
levels.303.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Wait—the column’s 2 can only sit at a6 or b6, so the box’s other cells cannot be 2. With 2 eliminated, a4 is 6.
levels.303.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! That is a Box Block—the column constrains the box, the box deletes the rest.
levels.303.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Great! Now e6: the row has 9, 7, 4, 2, 1, 8, the column has 1, 5, 6, the box still has 1, 6, 2, 8—only 3 remains. Enter 3!
Again! With e6 filled, look at e4: the box now has 1, 6, 2, 8, 3, the row has 9, 7, 4, 2, 1, 8, the column has 1, 8, 4—only 5 remains. Enter 5!
levels.303.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the Box Block method to find two more numbers.
levels.304.lesson.phases.intro.text: Nine-region review: on a 9×9 board, every row, column, and box sums to 45 (Star-Balance); each cage’s numbers total its corner label. Bring out all these weapons.
levels.304.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: Look at b7: it shares a cage summing to 16 with c7.
levels.304.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: b7 is already 7, so c7 = 16 − 7 = 9! A direct application of the cage sum (a Star-Balance variant).
levels.304.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: 9×9 Star-Balance review: rows, columns, and boxes all sum to 45. Subtract knowns from 45 or from a cage sum to lock empty cells.
levels.304.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: Confirm c7: no 9 in its row, column, or box—entering 9 is safe.
levels.304.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Star-Balance review: a row/column/box sums to 45; a cage sums to its corner label. Subtract knowns from 45 or the cage sum to lock cells.
levels.304.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 2-cell cage sums to 16 and the other cells add up to 7—subtract what's filled: what should c7 be?
levels.304.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Wait—this cage totals 16, b7 is already 7, so c7 = 16 − 7 = 9.
levels.304.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! Cage sum plus Star-Balance—two blades as one.
levels.304.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Great! Now e8: the row has 3, 5, 1, 8, the column has 8, 2, 9, 6, 4, the box still has 1, 8, 9—only 7 remains. Enter 7!
Again! c1: the row has 7, 8, 2, the column has 6, 5, 8, 3, 9, the box still has 6, 5, 8, 4, 7—only 1 remains. Enter 1!
levels.304.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use Star-Balance and elimination to find two more numbers.
levels.304.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: The nine regions are yours—the rest is up to you.
levels.305.lesson.phases.intro.text: Naked Pair: in the same row, column, or box, two cells can only hold the same two numbers—those numbers are locked by them, and no other cell can take them.
levels.305.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: Look at row 1. Only three cells remain: a4, a5, a6.
levels.305.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: These two cells form a Naked Pair: 2 and 3 are firmly locked by them, so no other cell in this row can be 2 or 3.
levels.305.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: So a5 can never be 2 or 3—after elimination, only 1 remains. Enter 1!
levels.305.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Naked Pair in three steps: find two cells with identical candidates in one region; lock those two numbers; eliminate them from the region’s other cells.
levels.305.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: a4 and a6 share candidates 2, 3, forming a Naked Pair—after ruling out 2 and 3 from a5, what remains? Try it.
levels.305.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Wait—a4 and a6 lock 2 and 3, so a5 cannot be 2 or 3. Of a5’s candidates 1, 2, 3, only 1 remains.
levels.305.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! That is a Naked Pair—two cells lock two numbers, everything around is eliminated.
levels.305.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Great! Now column 2: e2 and g2 share candidates 5, 6—another Naked Pair. i2’s candidates 1, 6 lose the 6—leaving 1. Enter 1!
Again! c4’s candidates are 2 and 8. In the top-right box, 2 can only sit at c7 and c8 (both in row c)—the Row Block rules 2 out of row c outside the box, leaving c4 as 8. Enter 8!
levels.305.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use Naked Pair and block elimination to find two more numbers.
levels.306.lesson.phases.intro.text: Technique combination: block elimination, Naked Pair, and Star-Balance all on stage. Find the key locking pattern first, then close the net with elimination.
levels.306.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: Look at row 3. Cells c4 and c6 both have candidates 5 and 7.
levels.306.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: They form another Naked Pair—5 and 7 locked in these two cells, so no other cell in this row can be 5 or 7.
levels.306.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: Look at c2: its candidates were 4 and 5—the Naked Pair eliminates 5, leaving only 4. Enter 4!
levels.306.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: This is technique combination: a Naked Pair narrows the range, then row/column/box elimination and Star-Balance close the net.
levels.306.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Technique combination: first find locking patterns like Naked Pair and blocks, then use elimination (with Star-Balance) to close the net step by step.
levels.306.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: c4 and c6 lock 5 and 7—after ruling 5 out of c2’s candidates (4, 5), what is left? Try it.
levels.306.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Wait—c4 and c6 form a Naked Pair locking 5 and 7, so c2 cannot be 5. Of c2’s candidates 4 and 5, only 4 remains.
levels.306.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! The Naked Pair unlocks, and combined techniques shine.
levels.306.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Great! Now b2: the row has 6, 3, 4, 7, the column has 9, 8, 7, 3, 2, the box still has 7, 9, 1, 6, 8—only 5 remains. Enter 5!
Again! With b2 filled, look at b1: candidates are 2 and 5, and the row already has 5—leaving 2. Enter 2!
levels.306.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Combine various techniques to find two more numbers.
levels.307.lesson.phases.intro.text: Chapter 3 final trial. Star-Balance, block elimination, Naked Pair—combine every technique you have learned.
levels.307.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: Combine all techniques, starting from the most constrained cell.
levels.307.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: e8: the row has 3, 8, 7, the column has 7, 9, 4, 1, 5, the box still has 4, 7, 6, 1—only 2 remains.
levels.307.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Start from the most constrained cell: eliminate row by row, column, box, using cage sums and Naked Pairs when needed.
levels.307.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! Combine every technique and keep pushing.
levels.307.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use combined techniques to find two more cells.
levels.307.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: The trial begins—combine all techniques to solve this level.
levels.401.lesson.phases.intro.text: Shen Mo steps into corridor B1. Old scratches line the stone walls, and a fresh mud print marks the floor. He records everything he sees on paper—position, direction, age. Notes are the only thing you can trust underground. Eyes miss things; notes do not.
levels.401.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Look at row 1: 9, 1, 3, 7, 5, and 4 are filled, leaving 2, 6, 8.
levels.401.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: Now the box this cell sits in (box 2): 7, 5, 8, 4, 3, 2, 1 are filled, lacking only 6 and 9.
levels.401.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: This cell is in both row 1 and this box: the row lacks 2, 6, 8, the box lacks 6, 9—the overlap leaves only 6!
levels.401.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: This is what notes are for: mark the candidates and the intersection becomes obvious. Tap the ✏️ Notes button, then tap the cell to mark candidates.
levels.401.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: This cell now has only one candidate, 6—enter 6!
levels.401.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Systematic notes in three steps: 1) scan each row/column/box for missing numbers; 2) mark every empty cell’s possible candidates; 3) find the overlap—where only one candidate remains, that is the answer.
levels.401.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 3-cell cage sums to 18 with 0 already filled, so a6 must pair with the remaining empty cells to make 18. Eliminate what the row/column/box rules out—what's left is your answer. Try it.
levels.401.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Wait, check again: this cell’s row lacks 2, 6, 8 and its box lacks 6, 9—the intersection is a single number. Enter 6.
levels.401.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! That is the power of systematic notes—mark the candidates and the answer jumps out.
levels.401.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Great! Once more: this cell’s column lacks 1, 2, its box lacks 1, 4, 7, 8, its row lacks 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9—the intersection is 1. Enter 1!
Nice! Keep going: this cell’s only candidate is 1 (column lacks 1, 4, 7, 8; box lacks 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9; row lacks 1, 2, 6, 8, 9)—enter 1!
levels.401.lesson.phases.noteToFill.hint: Now practice note-taking: select the empty cell in row 5, column 8 and mark its candidates (3, 4, 8—start with 3 and 8). Tap ✏️ to enter note mode!
levels.401.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the same method—note first, then fill—to find two certain cells.
levels.401.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: Systematic notes mastered! Every advanced technique from here depends on it.
levels.402.lesson.phases.intro.text: The number 7 can only sit in one spot in box 3. Not because it is obvious—but because every other place is already taken. The deepest-hidden number is usually the one squeezed out by the most constraints.
levels.402.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Look at the middle-left box (box 4): it has 1, 6, 3, 7, lacking 2, 4, 5, 8, 9. First scan where the number 5 can go.
levels.402.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: Among five empty cells, only this one can hold 5! Even though it has many notes (2, 4, 5), the number 5 has only one spot in the whole box—this is Hidden Single! Enter 5!
levels.402.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: How to find a Hidden Single: do not stare at one cell—scan number by number. Ask: how many spots can this number take in this row/column/box? If only one remains, fill it.
levels.402.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the number 5 can only go in one spot in the middle-left box (box 4). Find it and try.
levels.402.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Take your time: check each cell’s candidates in the middle-left box—which one is the only place for 5?
levels.402.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! That is Hidden Single—Lone Star looks at cells, Hidden Radiance looks at numbers!
levels.402.lesson.phases.guided.successN: One more: the number 9 can only go in one cell of row 9 (no other empty cell has 9). Find it and enter 9!
Keep going: the number 6 also appears in only one spot in row 7. Enter 6!
levels.402.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Keep using number-by-number scanning to find two more numbers.
levels.402.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: Hidden Single mastered! Remember: Lone Star looks at cells, Hidden Radiance looks at numbers.
levels.403.lesson.phases.intro.text: Two numbers in the same region can only land in the same two cells. You do not know which cell takes which number—but you do know that once this pair of positions is locked, these numbers appear nowhere else.
levels.403.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Look at the bottom-left box (box 7). First scan the numbers 5 and 7—where can each go?
levels.403.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: This cell’s candidates are 2, 5, 6, 7, 8—it contains 5 and 7.
levels.403.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: This cell’s candidates are 5, 6, 7—it also contains 5 and 7.
levels.403.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: This cell’s candidates are 6, 8—neither 5 nor 7. The other cells likewise hold no 5 or 7.
levels.403.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: So in the bottom-left box, 5 and 7 can only sit in (6,0) and (7,0)—this is a Hidden Pair! Now row 8: no other empty cell has 7.
levels.403.lesson.phases.demo.steps.6.te: So (7,0) must be 7! The Hidden Pair locks the positions, and the answer emerges. Enter 7!
levels.403.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: How to find a Hidden Pair: scan number pairs. Pick two numbers and see where each can go in a row/column/box—if both land in the same two cells, the pair is locked; delete all candidates except these two from those cells.
levels.403.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: in the bottom-left box, which two cells lock 5 and 7? Combine that with row 8 to pin one of them—try it.
levels.403.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Think again: only two cells in the bottom-left box contain 5 and 7, occupying both spots; only one cell in row 8 has 7—that is it.
levels.403.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! A Hidden Pair is not about filling—it is about elimination: lock one pair and every other candidate yields!
levels.403.lesson.phases.guided.successN: The Hidden Pair’s other half is set: 5 and 7 are locked in (6,0) and (7,0); (7,0) is already 7, so (6,0) must be 5!
levels.403.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Keep using pair-by-pair scanning to find two more numbers.
levels.403.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: Hidden Pair mastered! Both forms of the pair—Naked Pair and Hidden Pair—are yours now.
levels.404.lesson.phases.intro.text: Three cells, three candidate sets, together forming exactly three distinct numbers. They can swap positions, but never leave these cells. Find them and the space around them loosens.
levels.404.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Look at the middle-left box (box 4). Mark notes first, then observe: do three cells’ candidates together form exactly three numbers?
levels.404.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: This cell’s only candidate is 7. Together the three cells form exactly {2, 6, 7}!
levels.404.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: This is a Naked Triple: 2, 6, 7 are locked in these three cells, so no other cell can hold them. Look at this cell: its candidates were 2, 4, and 2 is eliminated—only 4 remains!
levels.404.lesson.phases.demo.steps.6.te: Enter 4! One Naked Triple elimination sweeps a row of notes clean.
levels.404.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: How to find a Naked Triple: in a row/column/box, find three cells whose candidates together form exactly three distinct numbers (each cell need not have all three). Lock them, then delete these three numbers from other cells in the region.
levels.404.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: in the middle-left box, {2, 6, 7} are locked in three cells. Find the cell left with a single candidate—try it.
levels.404.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Observe again: this cell’s candidates were 2, 4, and the Naked Triple eliminates 2—what is left?
levels.404.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! The Naked Triple locks 2, 6, 7 into three cells, sweeping the other notes clean.
levels.404.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Chain reaction: in the same box, another cell’s candidates were 1, 2, and the 2 is also eliminated—leaving 1. Enter 1!
levels.404.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Keep looking for Naked Triple patterns to pin two more numbers.
levels.404.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: Naked Triple mastered! From pairs to triples, your reasoning arsenal grows.
levels.405.lesson.phases.intro.text: A cage’s sum constraint is tighter than rows or columns. A set of cells must total a fixed value—meaning some numbers can never appear here from the start.
levels.405.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Look at this three-cell cage summing to 17. It already holds 4 at (1,3), so the remaining two cells must total 13.
levels.405.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: Two cells totaling 13 can only be {4, 9}, {5, 8}, or {6, 7}—so (2,3) can only be 5 or 8.
levels.405.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: Now row 3: it already has a 5 (at (2,7)). So (2,3) cannot be 5!
levels.405.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: Eliminate 5 from the combinations and only 8 remains—(2,3) is 8! The cage sum is the sharpest elimination tool!
levels.405.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: In-cage elimination in three steps: 1) list all possible combinations from the cage sum and cell count; 2) eliminate candidates using existing row/column/box numbers; 3) if only one number remains, fill it.
levels.405.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 3-cell cage sums to 17 with 4 already filled, so c4 must pair with the remaining empty cells to make 13. Eliminate what the row/column/box rules out—what's left is your answer. Try it.

levels.405.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! Cage combination plus in-row elimination pins a number.
levels.405.lesson.phases.guided.successN: The cage’s other half: the two remaining cells are 5 and 8, and (2,3) is already 8, so this cell is 5!

levels.406.lesson.phases.intro.text: Every technique lives in this one puzzle. Row, column, box, cage sum, difference, Naked Pair, Hidden Single, blocks—all of them. You need no new tricks, just everything you already know.
levels.406.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Look at this four-cell cage summing to 19: 2 and 1 are filled, leaving two cells totaling 16—only {7, 9}.
levels.406.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: Now the top-right box: 7 already sits at (2,8), so (1,8) cannot be 7.
levels.406.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: Eliminate 7 from {7, 9} and only 9 remains—(1,8) is 9! Cage, box, and row intersect; the answer has nowhere to hide.

levels.501.lesson.phases.intro.text: Nested cages—a big cage wrapping smaller ones. Find the innermost cell first. Once it is set, the outer layer can be unwrapped. Key 4 is the start of entering No. 94.
levels.501.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Find the innermost cage first—the single-cell cage. Its sum is the number to fill: sum 7, so (1,6) is directly 7.
levels.501.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: Set the innermost value first, like peeling an onion to its core.
levels.501.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: Now the two-cell cage wrapping it, sum 6. It already holds 5—subtract the inner known sum from the big cage sum, and what remains is the middle cell’s value.
levels.501.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: 6 − 5 = 1, so (2,2) must be 1! Peel layer by layer and the middle value emerges.
levels.501.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Nested cage method: find the innermost layer first (a single-cell cage fixes its value), then use “cage sum − known cells = remaining value” outward layer by layer.
levels.501.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 2-cell cage sums to 6 and the other cells add up to 5—subtract what's filled: what should c3 be?
levels.501.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Think again: this cage sums to 6, with 5 already inside—what is 6 − 5?
levels.501.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! You have learned to subtract the inner known sum from the big cage sum—the core of nested cages.
levels.501.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Great! Try one more: a cage summing to 18 already holds 7 and 3—what fills this cell?

levels.502.lesson.phases.intro.text: Irregular cages—they can be misshapen and cross box boundaries. But the sum rule never changes. Shape is only appearance; the sum is the core constraint.
levels.502.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Look at this five-cell cage summing to 21—it snakes from the top-middle box into the top-right box. This is an irregular cage.
levels.502.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: Look at its part inside the top-right box: this box has only two whole cages, summing to 24 and 13, for a total of 37. Box sum 45 − 37 = 8.
levels.502.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: So the two cells crossing into the box, (0,6) and (0,7), must total 8. Row 0 already has 3, 9, 7, leaving {1,2,4,5,6,8}—only 2 and 6 can form 8.
levels.502.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: Now (0,7)’s column: it already has 2, 8, 7, 9, so 2 is impossible—therefore (0,7)=6 and (0,6)=2!
levels.502.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: Irregular cages are nothing to fear: segment, subtract, eliminate—the answer appears.
levels.502.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Handling cross-box irregular cages: segment at box boundaries → subtract the in-box whole-cage sums from 45 to get the crossing segment’s sum → use row/column elimination to lock the exact numbers.
levels.502.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: (0,6) and (0,7) total 8, row 0 leaves {1,2,4,5,6,8}, and (0,7)’s column already has 2—so try (0,6).
levels.502.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Double-check: (0,6)+(0,7)=8, and only {2,6} in row 0 forms 8; since (0,7)’s column already has 2, (0,6) must be 2.
levels.502.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! The cross-box irregular cage is dismantled by your Star-Balance difference.
levels.502.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Great! One more drill: a two-cell cage summing to 6 holds 2—what fills this cell?

levels.503.lesson.phases.intro.text: Compound cages—multiple cages overlap and cross, sharing the same cells. Break down each cage’s constraint first, then merge them at the shared cells.
levels.503.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Look at cage 21, sum 13. It already holds (5,1)=4—so (5,0)+(6,0) must total 9.
levels.503.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: The 4 is the pivot of the system: cage 21’s constraint instantly shrinks to two cells.
levels.503.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: Look at (6,0): after row 6, column 0, and box elimination, candidates are only {1,6,8}; (5,0)’s candidates are only {7,8}. The pair must total 9—only 8+1 works, so (6,0)=1 and (5,0)=8.
levels.503.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: Cage 24 is the same: sum 18, holding (6,6)=3 and (7,7)=6.
levels.503.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: 18 − 3 − 6 = 9, so (6,7) is 9! Link multiple cage sums—set one cell and the rest loosen.
levels.503.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Compound cage linking: cage sum − known cells = remaining sum; then combine with row/column/box candidate elimination to lock the unique combination.
levels.503.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: cage 21 sums to 13 with 4 filled, leaving (5,0)+(6,0)=9; (6,0)’s candidates are {1,6,8}, (5,0)’s are {7,8}—try (6,0).
levels.503.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Think again: only 8+1 can total 9, (5,0) must be 8, so (6,0) is 1.
levels.503.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! You linked the compound cages’ sum constraints.
levels.503.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Great! Keep linking: a cage summing to 17 holds 9—this cell is 8!

levels.504.lesson.phases.intro.text: Multi-box Star-Balance—when one box is not enough, look at two or three. Stack the sums and differences surface. The wider your view, the clearer the answer.
levels.504.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: First the top-left box. Cages fully inside it sum to 14, 9, and 16—a total of 39. Box sum 45 − 39 = 6—the box’s only uncovered cell, (2,2), is 6!
levels.504.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: The single-box Star-Balance 45 rule fixes (2,2)=6 first.
levels.504.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: Now the top-middle box: whole cages sum to 26 and 10, totaling 36. 45 − 36 = 9, so (0,5), (1,5), (2,5) total 9; 2 and 3 are filled, so (2,5)=4.
levels.504.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: Finally verify by joining both boxes—this is the 90 rule: the two boxes’ whole cages sum to 75, leaving the four crossing cells (0,5), (1,5), (2,5), (2,2) totaling 15; with 2 and 3 known, (2,2)+(2,5)=10, exactly 6+4—two Star-Balance paths converge!
levels.504.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Star-Balance Law: a single box always sums to 45; subtract its whole-cage sums and what remains is the uncovered cells’ total; with one cell left, fix it directly.
levels.504.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the top-left box’s whole cages sum to 39, leaving only (2,2)—try 45 − 39.

levels.504.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Great! Top-middle box: 45 − 36 = 9, with 2 and 3 filled—what goes in (2,5)?

levels.505.lesson.phases.demo.steps.6.te: Look at (6,4): row 6 has 3, 7, 6, 5, 1, and column 4 with the box eliminate further—only 8 remains. Enter 8! Combine techniques and lock cells one by one.

levels.601.lesson.phases.intro.text: Deep nested cages—cages wrapped layer within layer. Break the innermost one and the outside loosens. Find the innermost number and the whole chain opens in sequence.
levels.601.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Look at this three-cell cage: sum 14. The left cell (4,1) holds 8, so the remaining pair totals 14−8=6—only {1,5} or {2,4}.
levels.601.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: Look at row 5, where (5,0) sits: it has 6 and 1, lacking {2,3,4,5,7,8,9}—the 1 in {1,5} is eliminated.
levels.601.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: Now column 0: it has 5, 1, 2—candidates 1, 2, and 5 are all eliminated.
levels.601.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: Of {1,5} and {2,4}, row and column elimination leave only 4—(5,0) is 4! The cage difference plus cross constraints confirm twice.
levels.601.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Endgame method: read the cage sum and filled cells, compute the remaining total, enumerate combinations; then eliminate candidates one by one with row, column, and box constraints—what remains is the answer.

levels.602.lesson.phases.intro.text: Big cage sums—the bigger the cage, the more candidates. But the sum is fixed. Lock the total first, then work cell by cell, and the range narrows step by step.
levels.602.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Look at row 1: 3, 7, 6, 4, 2, 5, 1, 9—eight numbers present, so the row lacks only an 8.
levels.602.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: The cell to fill belongs to this five-cell cage “sum 31”—it spans the middle of column 6. Big-cage combos are many, but row 1’s constraint locks 8 right into this cell.
levels.602.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: The row’s only missing 8 falls inside the big cage—the cage combos and row constraint confirm each other: combos without 8 are discarded, and (1,6) is 8! This is the big cage’s cross constraint.
levels.602.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Solving big-cage mysteries: enumerate the sum combinations first, then use cross constraints among row, column, box, and cage to eliminate candidates and lock the unique value.

levels.603.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: Column 0 also has 5 and 2—(6,0) cannot be 2.
levels.603.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: 3−2=1, and the cage complement plus column elimination confirm twice—(6,0) is 1! This is the first step of extreme reasoning: chain cage, pair, and elimination together.
levels.603.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Extreme reasoning essentials: every time you fix a number, immediately update the candidates of its row, column, box, and cage, chaining “in-cage pair → elimination → new fix” into a reasoning chain, step by step.

levels.701.lesson.phases.intro.text: Naked Pair, deepened—two numbers locked in one pair of cells. Lock them and confirm they are not replaced. Like verifying a file has not been touched—same position, same order, still itself.
levels.701.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Look at column 7. Mark every cell’s candidates with notes, then search: do any two cells share identical candidates?
levels.701.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: Cell g7: candidates are only 2 and 7.
levels.701.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: Cell h7: candidates are also only 2 and 7! Two cells, exactly two identical candidates—a Naked Pair is formed!
levels.701.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: 2 and 7 are locked by g7 and h7: no other cell in column 7 can be 2 or 7.
levels.701.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: The same holds in the bottom-right box: 2 and 7 belong only to these two cells. Two cells lock two numbers; everything around is eliminated.
levels.701.lesson.phases.demo.steps.6.te: Look at g6: it sits in the bottom-right box; combining row, column, box, and Naked Pair elimination, its candidates narrow—only 5 remains. Enter 5!
levels.701.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Naked Pair in three steps: find two cells in the same region with identical candidates; lock those two numbers; eliminate them from other cells in the region, then see what settles.
levels.701.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 3-cell cage sums to 14 and the other cells add up to 9—subtract what's filled: what should g7 be?
levels.701.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Wait—g7 and h7 already lock 2 and 7, so g6 cannot be 2 or 7. Look at its row, column, and box: 5 is the only way out.
levels.701.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! A Naked Pair is not just about two cells—lock one pair and the whole region’s candidates are swept clean.
levels.701.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Great! Now row 1: after row, column, and box elimination, (0,6) is only 9—try it.
Again! (1,1)’s candidates narrow to only 7—try it.
levels.701.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use Naked Pair and elimination to find two more numbers.
levels.701.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: Naked Pair mastered! The rest is yours.
levels.702.lesson.phases.intro.text: Hidden Single, deepened—scan numbers. When a number has only one spot left in a row, column, or box, that is the answer. When traces are cleaned to a single one, that trace matters most.
levels.702.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Look at column 5. For a Hidden Pair, “look at numbers, not cells”: scan each number and see which cells it can reach in this column.
levels.702.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: Number 5: in column 5 it can only sit at (7,5) and (8,5).
levels.702.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: Number 8: it can also only sit at (7,5) and (8,5)! Two numbers, the same two cells—a Hidden Pair appears!
levels.702.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: 5 and 8 are locked into these two cells: they can only be 5 and 8, and no other candidate can squeeze in.
levels.702.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: Now the remaining cells of column 5: where can 9 go? (0,5) only has {4,6}, and (2,5) is 4—only (5,5) can hold 9. Enter 9!
levels.702.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: How to find a Hidden Pair: scan number pairs. Pick two numbers and see where each can go in a row/column/box—if both land in the same two cells, the pair is locked; delete other candidates from those cells.
levels.702.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the Hidden Pair locks 5 and 8 into (7,5) and (8,5). Which cell in column 5 can hold 9? Try it.
levels.702.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Think again: in column 5, 5 and 8 can only be at (7,5) and (8,5), so 9 cannot be there; after ruling out (0,5)’s {4,6}, 9 has only (5,5).
levels.702.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! A Hidden Pair is not about filling—it is about elimination: lock one pair and every other candidate yields!
levels.702.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Great! Row 4 has only two empty cells, exactly {5,9}—try it.
The Hidden Pair’s other half is set: row 4’s remaining (4,8)—try it.
levels.702.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Keep using pair-by-pair scanning to find two more numbers.
levels.702.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: Hidden Pair mastered! Both forms of the pair—Naked Pair and Hidden Pair—are yours now.
levels.703.lesson.phases.intro.text: Naked Triple, deepened—three cells share three numbers. When three cells’ candidates together form exactly three distinct numbers, those three are locked. Like three coordinates converging into a single intersection.
levels.703.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Look at row 2. With notes marked, find the Naked Triple: three cells whose candidates together form exactly three distinct numbers.
levels.703.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: (1,5) is likewise {2, 4, 7}—the three cells together form exactly 2, 4, 7—a Naked Triple is formed!
levels.703.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: 2, 4, 7 are locked into these three cells; no other cell in row 2 can hold them. Look at (1,4): its candidates had 2, now eliminated—only 1 remains!
levels.703.lesson.phases.demo.steps.6.te: Enter 1! One Naked Triple elimination sweeps a whole row of notes clean.
levels.703.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: How to find a Naked Triple: in a row/column/box, find three cells whose candidates together form exactly three distinct numbers (each cell need not have all three). Lock them, then delete these three numbers from other cells in the region.
levels.703.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: in row 2, {2, 4, 7} are locked into (1,2), (1,3), (1,5). Find the cell left with a single candidate—try it.
levels.703.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Observe again: this cell’s candidates had 2, eliminated by the Naked Triple—what is left?
levels.703.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! The Naked Triple locks 2, 4, 7 into three cells, sweeping the other notes clean.
levels.703.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Chain reaction: in the same row, (1,6) narrows to only 8 after row, column, and box elimination—try it.
Again! (2,3)’s candidates narrow to only 5—try it.
levels.703.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Keep looking for Naked Triple patterns to pin two more numbers.
levels.703.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: Naked Triple mastered! From pairs to triples, your reasoning arsenal grows.
levels.704.lesson.phases.intro.text: X-Wing—two rows, two columns, four endpoints forming a rectangle. When a number in two rows can only sit in the same two columns, every other position is eliminated. Set the four corners and the middle opens.
levels.704.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Pick a number, say 6. First mark row by row: which cells can 6 reach in each row?
levels.704.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: In row 4, the 6 can only sit at (4,3) or (4,5).
levels.704.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: Now (4,5)—the row’s 6 hides between these two cells.
levels.704.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: Look at row 7: the 6 can also only sit at (6,3) or (6,5)—exactly the same two columns as the previous row!
levels.704.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: The shared columns emerge: c3 and c5.
levels.704.lesson.phases.demo.steps.6.te: The four corners (4,3), (4,5), (6,3), (6,5) form a rectangle—this is an X-Wing!
levels.704.lesson.phases.demo.steps.7.te: The 6 is locked into this rectangle: either at (4,3) and (6,5), or at (4,5) and (6,3). With row, column, and box elimination, the 6 at e5 ((4,5)) is settled—enter 6!
levels.704.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: X-Wing checklist: ① pick a number ② mark its possible cells row by row ③ find two rows sharing the same two columns ④ eliminate the number from other rows in those columns. You can also start from columns.
levels.704.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 3-cell cage sums to 12 and the other cells add up to 6—subtract what's filled: what should e6 be?
levels.704.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Think again: 6 can only appear in the four corners (4,3), (4,5), (6,3), (6,5). Look at e5’s row, column, and box—after eliminating other numbers, 6 is the answer.
levels.704.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! The X-Wing’s wings spread—lock two rows and two columns, and every other position yields!
levels.704.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Great! The rectangle’s opposite corner is set: g3 ((6,3)) is also 6—try it.
Again! e3 ((4,3)): with 6 placed, elimination leaves only 7—try it.
levels.704.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Keep using the X-Wing approach (pick a number → mark row by row → find the rectangle) to pin two more numbers.
levels.704.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: X-Wing mastered! You have officially entered the realm of pattern reasoning.
levels.705.lesson.phases.intro.text: Swordfish—three rows and three columns interwoven into a net. When the net closes, every excess path is sealed. Nine cells interlock into a complete closed structure.
levels.705.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: The Swordfish is the three-row version of the X-Wing. Pick a number, say 3, and mark its only possible spots row by row.
levels.705.lesson.phases.demo.steps.2.te: In row 4, the 3 can only land among the group at (3,5)—all within columns 4, 5, and 8.
levels.705.lesson.phases.demo.steps.3.te: Row 6: the 3 can also only sit in the same three columns (c4, c5, c8).
levels.705.lesson.phases.demo.steps.4.te: Look at (5,8)—one of the 3’s landing spots in this row.
levels.705.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: Row 7: the 3 still can only sit in these three columns! Three rows and three columns interweave into a net.
levels.705.lesson.phases.demo.steps.6.te: (6,4) is also a corner of the net.
levels.705.lesson.phases.demo.steps.7.te: The first of the three columns: c4.
levels.705.lesson.phases.demo.steps.9.te: The third column: c8. Three rows and three columns form the net—a Swordfish is formed!
levels.705.lesson.phases.demo.steps.10.t: The 3 is caught in this net, appearing only in the three columns of these three rows. Look at d5 ((3,5)): with the net and row, column, box elimination, the 3 settles here—enter 3!
levels.705.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: How to find a Swordfish: pick a number and record candidates row by row; if three rows’ candidates all lie in the same set of three columns (2-3 spots per row), lock those columns and eliminate the number from other rows in them.
levels.705.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the Swordfish locks 3 into rows d, f, g and columns c4, c5, c8. Look at d5 ((3,5))—with row, column, and box elimination, try it.
levels.705.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Think again: 3 can only appear in rows d, f, g at columns c4, c5, c8. Look at d5’s row, column, and box—after eliminating other numbers, 3 is the answer.
levels.705.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! The Swordfish dives in—once the three-by-three net forms, the number is cleared from the whole sea!
levels.705.lesson.phases.guided.successN: Great! Another corner of the net is set: g4 ((6,4))—try it.
Again! f8 ((5,8)): the Swordfish’s third corner—try it.
levels.705.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Keep scanning number by number for three-by-three coverage patterns to pin two more numbers.
levels.705.lesson.phases.free.unlockText: Swordfish conquered! You have mastered one of the most powerful advanced patterns.
levels.706.lesson.phases.intro.text: The master of secret arts—Naked Pair, Hidden Single, Triple, X-Wing, and Swordfish, all five patterns fused into one puzzle. Learn nothing new; walk all five roads as one. In this final puzzle, you will use every technique at once.
levels.706.lesson.phases.demo.steps.0.te: A synthesis puzzle has no single technique—start with the most direct observation. Look at row 1.
levels.706.lesson.phases.demo.steps.1.te: Find the Lone Star first: row 1, column 4, and the top-left box eliminate every other spot for 1, leaving (0,4) with a single candidate—enter 1.
levels.706.lesson.phases.guided.failHint: Start from the most constrained row, column, box, or cage, and push forward with the techniques you have learned.
levels.706.lesson.phases.guided.successT: Correct! Keep advancing with the five secret arts.
levels.706.lesson.phases.semiAuto.hintTe: Use the secret arts to find two more cells.

levels.204.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: On a 9×9 board, every row, column, and box always sums to 45. Subtract the sum of the known digits in that row/column/box from 45, and the remainder is the value of the empty cell.
levels.206.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: When two cages are nested, use the difference of their sums: subtract the smaller cage sum from the larger cage sum, and the remainder is the sum of the cells that belong only to the larger cage.
levels.206.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 2-cell cage sums to 12 and the other cells add up to 4—subtract what's filled: what should c5 be?
levels.207.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: When a cage crosses a box boundary, first take the box total of 45, then subtract the sums of the cages fully inside the box; the remainder is the value of the cell outside the box (outie).
levels.207.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 3-cell cage sums to 13 and the other cells add up to 4—subtract what's filled: what should c4 be?
levels.307.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: This is the Chapter 3 comprehensive trial—no new techniques. Use the Star Balance rule, pointing/claiming, and naked pairs, starting from the most constrained cell.
levels.307.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 5-cell cage sums to 20 with 12 already filled, so e8 must pair with the remaining empty cells to make 8. Eliminate what the row/column/box rules out—what's left is your answer. Try it.
levels.406.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: This is the Chapter 4 comprehensive recall: rows, columns, boxes, cage sums, differences, pairs, hidden singles, and pointing all intersect—start from the cage with the tightest sum.
levels.406.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 4-cell cage sums to 19 and the other cells add up to 10—subtract what's filled: what should b9 be?
levels.506.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: This is the Chapter 5 comprehensive trial: nested, irregular, and compound cages plus multi-box Star Balance—difference is often the sharpest opening.
levels.506.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 3-cell cage sums to 11 with 4 already filled, so a5 must pair with the remaining empty cells to make 7. Eliminate what the row/column/box rules out—what's left is your answer. Try it.
levels.606.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: This is the finale trial—no new techniques. Use everything you've learned. For a single-cell cage, its sum is exactly the number to fill.
levels.606.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: i5 is a single-cell cage—its sum 5 IS the number to fill. What is it?
levels.706.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: This is the Chapter 7 comprehensive recall: naked pairs, hidden pairs, triples, X-Wing, and Swordfish all combined—begin with the most obvious row/column/box/cage.
levels.706.lesson.phases.guided.hintText: Your turn: the 4-cell cage sums to 15 with 10 already filled, so a5 must pair with the remaining empty cells to make 5. Eliminate what the row/column/box rules out—what's left is your answer. Try it.
levels.302.lesson.phases.demo.steps.6.te: Since 9 can only appear in column 5 inside the box, no cell of column 5 outside the box can be 9—including a5!
levels.302.lesson.phases.demo.steps.7.te: Look at a5: only 3 and 9 remain (mark 9 for now).
levels.302.lesson.phases.demo.steps.8.te: The Column Block eliminates 9 from a5.
levels.301.lesson.phases.demo.steps.6.te: Look at d3: only 4 and 8 remain (mark 4 for now).
levels.301.lesson.phases.demo.steps.7.te: The Row Block eliminates 4 from d3.
levels.303.lesson.phases.demo.steps.5.te: The Box Block eliminates 2 from a4.
levels.102.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Shen Mo's gaze moves to the small 2×2 box at the top-left of the board. Numbers 1–4 can't repeat inside the box either—cross out every digit already used in its row, column, and box; the one candidate left is the answer.
levels.103.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: The dashed outline is a cage, and the small number at its corner is the cage total. A one-cell cage holds a single empty cell—whatever it sums to is what you fill in; it is the easiest place to start.
levels.105.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: The smaller a two-cell cage total, the fewer ways to make it. Remember the key pairs: 3=1+2, 4=1+3, 6=2+4, 7=3+4—when the combo is unique, both cells are locked in at once.
levels.106.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: When lone singles run out, switch approach—scan the numbers. In a box (or row, or column), if a digit like 4 has only one empty cell left, that is a hidden single: every other spot is blocked, so it must go there.
levels.107.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: A quick refresher on unique combos: first break the cage total into its possible pairs, then use the row, column, and box to eliminate—once the illegal half is crossed out, the remaining cells write themselves.
levels.108.lesson.phases.guided.methodTe: Remember the key to a 4×4 board: every row, every column, and every box sums to exactly 10. When a row has just one empty cell left, subtract the filled cells total from 10—what remains is the answer.
